Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verses 1–3:

(p-154) (27. Surat al-Naml

Makkiyyah, and it has thirteen, or fourteen, or fifteen... [sic: the text reads "ثلاث أو أربع أو خمس وتسعون"] verses)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ta-Sin. These are the verses of the Qur'an and a Book that makes things clear.﴾ The demonstrative refers to the verses of the surah. The "Clear Book" is either the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), and its clarity lies in that what will occur is inscribed in it, so it makes it clear to those who look into it; its being placed later is by reference to our knowledge of it, and its being placed earlier in al-Hijr is by reference to existence. Or it refers to the Qur'an, and its clarity lies in what it has deposited within it of wisdoms and rulings. Or (it refers to the Qur'an) with respect to its soundness through its inimitability, and its conjunction with the Qur'an is like the conjunction of one of two attributes with the other; and its indefiniteness is for glorification. It was also read as "Kitabun" in the nominative, by omitting the genitive-governing noun and placing the noun in the genitive in its position.

﴿A guidance and good news for the believers.﴾ They are two circumstantial clauses (ḥāl) of "Āyāt," and the element governing them is the meaning of the demonstrative; or they are two substitutes (badal) for it; or two other predicates; or two predicates of an omitted subject.

﴿Who establish the prayer and give the zakat.﴾ "Who" refers to those who do the righteous deeds of prayer and zakat. ﴿And they, of the Hereafter, they are certain.﴾ It is a continuation of the relative clause, and the waw is for the circumstantial or for conjunction. The change in the construction serves to indicate the strength and steadfastness of their certainty, and that they are unique in it. Or it is a parenthetical sentence, as if it were said: "These who believe and do righteous deeds are the ones certain of the Hereafter," for the bearing of hardships occurs only out of fear of the consequence and reliance upon being held to account. The repetition of the pronoun is for exclusivity.

﴿When Moses said to his family, "Indeed I have perceived a fire."﴾ That is, mention his story: "when Moses said." It is also permissible for "idh" (when) to be connected to "ʿalīm" (knowing).

﴿I will bring you from it some news﴾, that is, about the state of the road, because he had lost his way. The pronoun is plural, although if it is sound that he had with him no one but his wife, then he referred to her by "family." The "sīn" (the prefix "sa-" of "sa-ātīkum") indicates the distance and the promise of coming, even if it is delayed.

﴿Or I will bring you a burning brand (qabas)﴾, that is, a lit flame of fire. The "shihāb" is made genitive by "qabas" because it may be a burning brand or not a burning brand. The Kufans and Yaʿqub (Yaʿqub al-Hadrami, a reader of the Qur'an) read it with tanwin (nunation), so that "qabas" is either a substitute (badal) for it or a descriptive adjective (waṣf) of it, because it carries the meaning of "the kindled one." The two promises are made by way of supposition, and for this reason he expressed them with the form of hope (tarajjī) in "Ṭā-Hā" (20:10). The alternation (tardīd) indicates that if he does not obtain them, he will not be deprived of one of the two, based on the outward appearance of the matter, or in confidence in God's custom, that He almost never combines two deprivations upon His servant.

﴿So that you may warm yourselves﴾, in hope that you may be warmed by it. "Al-ṣilā'" is the great fire.

When he came to it, he was called: ﴿Blessed is⦆ (i.e., "Blessed is"). The calling contains the sense of speech, or ﴿that blessed is⦆ may be read as *an* being a verbal particle (*an maṣdariyyah*) or the light form of *inna* (*mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah*, "lightened from the heavy"). Although lightening requires a substitute, such as *lā*, *qad*, *al-sīn*, or *sawfa*, this (*an*) is a supplication, and it differs from its counterparts in many rulings.

﴿Those in the fire and those around it⦆: *man* (those) is in the place of *al-nār* (the fire), which is the blessed spot mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed place⦆ (Qur'an 28:30). "Those around its place" refers to those around it. The apparent meaning is that it is general, covering everyone in that land and in that valley and around it, from the land of al-Shām (Greater Syria), which is marked with blessings because it was the place where the prophets were sent and where they were gathered, alive and dead, and especially that spot where God spoke to Mūsā. It has also been said that the intended meaning is Mūsā and the angels present. Beginning the address with this is a glad tiding that a great matter has been decreed for him, whose blessing will spread throughout the regions of al-Shām.

﴿And glory be to God, Lord of the worlds⦆ is part of what he was called with, lest it be imagined, from hearing His speech, that there is any likening (of God to creation). It also expresses wonder at the greatness of that matter. Or it is an expression of wonder by Mūsā at what overcame him of its greatness.

﴿O Mūsā, indeed it is I, God⦆: the *hā'* (in *innahu*) refers to the matter (*li-l-sha'n*), and "I am God" is a sentence explaining it. Or it refers to the speaker, with *anā* as its predicate and *Allāh* as an appositive (*bayān*) to it. ﴿The Mighty, the Wise⦆ are two attributes of God that prepare for what He intended to manifest. He means: I am the Powerful, the Capable over what is far from the imaginations, such as turning the staff into a serpent, the One who does everything I do with wisdom and planning.

﴿And throw down your staff﴾ is conjoined to (*būrika*, "blessed be"), meaning: it was called out, "that blessed is whoever is in the fire," and "that throw down your staff" (*an alqi ʿaṣāka*). This is shown by His saying ﴿and that throw down your staff﴾ after His saying ﴿that, O Moses, I am God﴾, with the repetition of *an*. ﴿When he saw it writhing﴾ means moving with agitation.

﴿As if it were a jinn﴾ means a small, quick snake. It was also read *jaʾn*, according to the dialect of those who hurried in fleeing from the meeting of two unvowelled letters (*iltiqāʾ al-sākinayn*, the clash of two consecutive silent consonants that Arabic avoids by adding a vowel or altering the form). ﴿He turned back fleeing and did not return﴾ means he did not come back, from *ʿaqqaba al-muqātil*, when a fighter returned to attack after fleeing. He was terrified only because he thought that this matter was intended against him. This is shown by His saying: ﴿O Moses, do not fear﴾, meaning, from anyone other than Me, out of trust in Me, or absolutely, due to His saying: ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾, meaning when revelation is sent to them, because of the intensity of their absorption, for they are the most fearful of people of God, the Exalted; or it means that they will have no evil consequence from Me, so they would fear it.

﴿Except one who has wronged, then substituted good after evil, indeed I am Forgiving, Merciful﴾ is a disconnected exception (*istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ*, an exception not of the same kind as what precedes it), by which he corrected what might occur to the mind about the negation of fear from all of them. Among them are some who committed a minor sin, and although they did it, they followed the act with what nullifies it, and thereby they deserve forgiveness and mercy from God, for He also does not cause them fear. It was intended as an allusion to Moses' striking of the Copt. It is also said that it is a connected exception, and there is a substitution (*badal*, a grammatical element that replaces and clarifies a preceding word) that is resumed (*mustaʾnaf*, a new clause not grammatically dependent on what precedes it), conjoined to something omitted, meaning: whoever has wronged, then substituted his sin with repentance.

﴿And insert your hand into your bosom﴾, because he was wearing a woolen cloak (mid'arat ṣūf) with no sleeves (lā kumma lahā, "it had no كُمّ"). For one who counts the staff and the hand among the nine, the last two may be counted as one, and he does not count the splitting, since he was not sent with it to Pharaoh.

Or: "go among nine signs," on the basis that it is a resumption (istinaf) concerning the sending, so that it is connected to it. ﴿To Pharaoh and his people﴾. On the first two readings, it is connected to something like مَبْعُوثًا (sent) or مُرْسَلًا (dispatched). ﴿Indeed they were a defiantly disobedient people﴾: this is a causal explanation (ta'līl) for the sending.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verses 13–14:

﴿So when Our signs came to them﴾ — that is, when Musa brought them to them. ﴿Manifest (mubsira)﴾ — clear (bayyina). It is an active participle (ism fa'il) used in the sense of a passive (ism maf'ul), indicating that because of their great visibility to the eyes, it is as though they would see themselves, were they among things that see; or it means possessing insight (dhat tabassur), in that they guide, while the blind cannot be guided, let alone guide others; or it means "making everyone who looks at them and reflects upon them see clearly." It is also read as "mabsara," meaning a place in which seeing (tabassur) abounds among you. ﴿They said, "This is clear magic."﴾ — whose magic nature is evident.

﴿And they denied them﴾ — and they rejected them. ﴿And their souls were convinced of them﴾ — and indeed their souls were convinced of them, because the waw here is for the circumstantial (li'l-hal). ﴿Out of wrongdoing﴾ — against their own selves. ﴿And arrogance﴾ — haughtiness (taraffu') in refusing faith. Both words are in the accusative of cause (ta'lil) governed by "jahadu" (they denied).

﴿So see how was the end of the corrupters﴾ — and that was drowning in this world and burning in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 15:

﴿And We certainly gave knowledge to Dawud and Sulayman﴾. [It was] a portion of knowledge, namely the knowledge of wisdom (hikam) and the sacred laws (shara'i'), or [it was] knowledge of whatever kind [i.e., knowledge in an unrestricted sense]. ﴿And they both said: "Praise be to Allah"﴾. He joined it with the conjunction "wa" (and) to indicate that what they said is part of what they did in return for this blessing, as if he had said: "So they acted, in gratitude to Him, with what they did, and they said: 'Praise be to Allah.'" ﴿Who has favoured us over many of His believing servants﴾. That is, over those who were not given knowledge or the like of their knowledge. In this there is evidence of the excellence of knowledge and the nobility of its people, since they gave thanks for knowledge and made it the basis of superiority, and did not regard as more important than it the kingdom they had been given, which was not given to anyone else besides them. It is also an exhortation to the scholar that he should praise Allah the Exalted for what He has granted him of His bounty, and that he should be humble and believe that, although he has been favoured over many, many have also been favoured over him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verses 16–17:

﴿And Sulayman inherited from Dawud﴾ prophethood, or knowledge, or kingship, by standing in his place in that, to the exclusion of the rest of his sons, who were nineteen in number. ﴿And he said: "O people, we have been taught the speech of the birds, and we have been given of everything"﴾ to publicize the blessing of God and to proclaim it, and to call people to believe by mentioning the miracle, which is the knowledge of the speech of the birds, and other great things that he was given. In common usage, "nutq" (speech) and "mantiq" (utterance) refer to every expression by which what is in the mind is conveyed, whether single or compound. It may also be applied, by way of analogy or extension, to anything that is produced as a sound, as in the saying "the dove spoke" (nataqat al-hamamah). From this comes the description of animate beings as "speaking" (natiq) and of inanimate things as "silent" (samit). The animal sounds, insofar as they follow from imaginings, are treated as expressions, especially since among them are sounds that vary according to differing purposes, such that those of the same species understand them.

Perhaps Sulayman, peace be upon him, whenever he heard the sound of an animal, knew by his holy power the imagining that produced its sound and the purpose he intended by it. Among this is what is related: that he passed by a nightingale that was chirping and dancing, and he said: "It says: when I eat half a date, then let the world perish." And a turtle-dove cried out, and he said: "It is saying: would that creation had not been created." Perhaps the nightingale's sound came from satiety and a carefree state, and the dove's cry from enduring hardship and the pain of the heart.

The pronoun in ("we have been taught") and ("we have been given") refers to him and to his father, peace be upon them both, but he began with himself alone, following the custom of kings, in observance of the rules of governance. The intended meaning of ﴿of everything﴾ is the abundance of what he was given, as in your saying: "So-and-so is sought by everyone and knows everything." ﴿Indeed, this is surely the manifest bounty﴾ which is hidden from no one.

﴿And his hosts were gathered for Sulayman, of the jinn and the humans and the birds, and they were marshalled﴾ they were held back, by holding back the first of them until the last of them, so that they would come together in order.

In common usage, "nutq" (speech) and "mantiq" (utterance) refer to every expression by which what is in the mind is conveyed, whether single or compound. It may also be applied, by way of analogy or extension, to anything that is produced as a sound, as in the saying "the dove spoke" (nataqat al-hamamah). From this comes the description of animate beings as "speaking" (natiq) and of inanimate things as "silent" (samit). The animal sounds, insofar as they follow from imaginings, are treated as expressions, especially since among them are sounds that vary according to differing purposes, such that those of the same species understand them.

Perhaps Sulayman, peace be upon him, whenever he heard the sound of an animal, knew by his holy power the imagining that produced its sound and the purpose he intended by it. Among this is what is related: that he passed by a nightingale that was chirping and dancing, and he said: "It says: when I eat half a date, then let the world perish." And a turtle-dove cried out, and he said: "It is saying: would that creation had not been created." Perhaps the nightingale's sound came from satiety and a carefree state, and the dove's cry from enduring hardship and the pain of the heart.

The pronoun in ("we have been taught") and ("we have been given") refers to him and to his father, peace be upon them both, but he began with himself alone, following the custom of kings, in observance of the rules of governance. The intended meaning of ﴿of everything﴾ is the abundance of what he was given, as in your saying: "So-and-so is sought by everyone and knows everything." ﴿Indeed, this is surely the manifest bounty﴾ which is hidden from no one.

﴿And his hosts were gathered for Sulayman, of the jinn and the humans and the birds, and they were marshalled﴾ they were held back, by holding back the first of them until the last of them, so that they would come together in order.

﴿Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants﴾: a valley in al-Sham (Greater Syria) with many ants. The verb is followed by (عَلى, "upon") either because their coming was from a height, or because what is meant is a part of the expression "atā ʿalā al-shayʾ" (he came upon the thing), meaning he exhausted it and reached its end, as if they wanted to descend to the far end of the valley.

﴿An ant said: "O ants, enter your dwellings"﴾: as if, when it saw them heading toward the valley, it fled from them out of fear of being trampled. Another ant followed it and cried out a cry by which it alerted the ants nearby, and they followed it. This was likened to addressing and advising rational beings, and that is why they were treated as such, although there is nothing to prevent God, glorified and exalted, from having created in them reason and speech.

﴿Let not Solomon and his hosts crush you﴾: a prohibition addressed to them against trampling. What is meant is the ant's prohibition against stopping in a way that would lead them to crush the ants, like the saying "I shall not see you here." It is either a resumed statement (istinaf, a new sentence) or a substitute (badal) for the command, and it has no response (jawab), since the energetic nūn (نَّ) does not enter it in the broad sense.

﴿while they do not perceive﴾: that they are crushing you. For had they perceived, they would not have done so. It is as if the ant perceived the infallibility of the prophets from injustice and harm. It was also said that it is a resumed statement, meaning: Solomon and the people are unaware.

﴿So he smiled, laughing, at her words﴾: in wonder at her caution, her warning, and her guidance to what is good for them, and in joy at what God, exalted, had singled him out with, namely perceiving her whispering and understanding her purpose. For this reason he asked for the grace to give thanks.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 20–21:

﴿And he inspected the birds﴾: he looked over (taʿarrafa) the birds, and did not find the hoopoe among them. ﴿So he said: "Why is it that I do not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent?"﴾ Here "am" (or) is disjunctive (munqatiʿah). It is as if, when he did not see it, he thought it was present but was not seeing it because of some screen or something else, so he said: "Why do I not see it?" Then he took precaution, and it became clear to him that it was absent, so he turned away from that and began to say: "Is it absent?", as if he were asking about the correctness of what had become clear to him.

﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment﴾: such as plucking out its feathers and casting it into the sun, or leaving it where ants will eat it, or placing it together with its opposite in a cage. ﴿Or I will surely slaughter him﴾: so that the members of its kind may take warning from it. ﴿Or he will bring me a clear authority﴾: with a proof that makes its excuse evident. Strictly speaking, the oath is sworn on one of the first two, on the assumption that the third does not occur. But since that required the occurrence of one of the three matters, he made the sworn-upon item triple by conjoining the third to the other two. Ibn Kathir read "aw la-yaʾtiyannani" (or, let him surely bring me) with two nuns, the first of which is open and doubled.

﴿And I have come to you from Saba'﴾. Ibn Kathir, in the transmission of al-Bazzi, and Abu ʿAmr read ﴿سَبَإٍ﴾ as ghayr maṣrūf (diptote, without tanwin), on the interpretation of it as a tribe or a town. Al-Qawwas read the hamza with sukūn (hamzah sākinah).

﴿with certain news﴾, with a verified report. It is narrated that when he (ﷺ) had finished building Bayt al-Maqdis (the Holy House in Jerusalem), he prepared for the Hajj, reached the Sacred Precinct (al-Ḥaram), and stayed there as long as he willed. Then he set out for Yemen, leaving Makkah in the morning, reached Ṣanʿāʾ at midday, and was pleased by the pleasantness of its land, so he alighted there. Then he found no water. The hoopoe (al-Hudhud) was his scout, because it is skilled at finding water.

So he searched for it for that purpose and did not find it, since it had flown up when Sulayman alighted. Then he saw a hoopoe settled, so he descended toward it, they exchanged descriptions, and he flew with it to see what it had described to him. Then it returned after the afternoon and related what it related. Perhaps among the wonders of God's power, and what He singled out for His special servants, there are things greater than that, which those who know them consider magnificent and which those who deny them find unbelievable.

I found a woman ruling over them, and she has been given of everything a king might need, and she has a mighty throne. (Bilqis, daughter of Sharahil, son of Malik, son of al-Rayyan; the pronoun refers to Saba' or to its people.)

"And she has been given of everything a king might need." "And she has a mighty throne": he described it as mighty in relation to her, or in relation to the thrones of women like her.

It is said that it was thirty cubits by thirty in breadth and height, or eighty by eighty, of gold and silver, adorned with jewels.

"I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah." It is as if they were worshipping it. "And Satan made their deeds appealing to them": the worship of the sun and other of their repugnant deeds. "And he averted them from the path": from the path of truth and right. "So they are not guided": to it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verses 25–26:

﴿Why do they not prostrate to God?﴾ He (Satan) barred them, so that they would not prostrate; or he (Satan) adorned for them (their deeds) that they should not prostrate. It is in apposition to (a‛mālahum, "their deeds"), or (lā yahtadūn, "they are not guided") to (an yasjudū, "that they prostrate"), with the addition of (lā, "not"). Al-Kisā'ī and Ya‛qūb read (alā, "why not/look") with light stress, on the basis that it is for alerting (tanbīh) and (yā, "O") for calling (nidā'), and its addressee is omitted, meaning: "Alā yā qawmi usjudū" (Look, O my people, prostrate), like his saying:

Ḥuwaiṭ / a poet's verse:
"She said: Alā yā isma‛ a‛izuka bi-khuṭṭatin... / So I said: Listening, speak and be right."

On this reading it is possible that it is a resumed statement (isti'nāf) from God or from Solomon, and the pause is on ﴿they are not guided﴾, so it becomes a command to prostrate. On the first (reading) it is a reproach for leaving it. On both readings it requires the obligation of prostration in general, not at the time of its recitation. It was also read (halla) and (hala) with the hamza changed to hā', and (alla tasjudūn) and (halla tasjudūn) in the second person (khiṭāb).

﴿Who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth, and knows what you conceal and what you disclose﴾: a description of Him, Exalted is He, with what necessitates His exclusive entitlement to prostration, by His singularity in perfect power and knowledge, as an exhortation to prostrate to Him and a refutation of those who prostrate to others. (al-khab' (the hidden)) is what is concealed in something else.

Its bringing forth (ikhrājuhu) is its manifestation, and it encompasses the shining of the stars, the sending down of rain, and the growing of plants, indeed also creation (inshā'), for it is bringing forth what is in a thing from potential to actuality, and origination (ibdā'), for it is bringing forth what is in possibility and non-existence into necessity and existence. It is known that this belongs specifically to the One necessary of existence in Himself. Ḥafṣ and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿what you conceal and what you disclose﴾ with the tā' (second person).

﴿God—there is no god but Him, Lord of the Mighty Throne﴾, which is the first and greatest of bodies and the one encompassing all of them; thus there is a great difference between the two "greats."

﴿He said: "We shall see"﴾ — sananzhuru, i.e. "we shall know" (sanaʿrif), taking naẓar in the sense of reflection (taʾammul). ﴿Have you spoken the truth, or have you been one of the liars?﴾ — i.e., "or have you lied?" ﴿She said: "Indeed, when kings enter a town﴾ by force and conquest. ﴿they ruin it﴾ — a disparagement of what she perceived of their inclination toward fighting, by their claim of inherent and accidental strengths, and an indication that she sees reconciliation as preferable, for fear that Sulayman would overstep their plans and hasten to destroy whatever of their wealth and buildings he came upon. Moreover, war is a game of chance (sijal), and one does not know its outcome. ﴿And they make the honored of its people humiliated﴾ by plundering their wealth, ravaging their homes, and other forms of humiliation and captivity. ﴿And thus they do﴾ — an emphasis on what she described of their condition, and an affirmation that this is among their established and constant customs; or it is a confirmation of her words from Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿And indeed, I am sending them a gift﴾ — an explanation of what she sees as the means of reconciliation. The meaning is: I am sending envoys with a gift, by which I will repel him from my kingdom. ﴿So I will wait to see what the envoys return with﴾ — regarding his condition, so that I may act according to it.

It is narrated that she sent Mundhir ibn Amr with a delegation, and she sent with them boys dressed in the garb of girls and girls dressed in the garb of boys, and a chest containing a virgin pearl and a bent-holed jasper, and she said: "If he is a prophet, he will distinguish between the boys and the girls, and will pierce the pearl with a straight hole and thread the bead with a string." When they reached his camp and saw the greatness of his affairs, their souls were humbled before him. When they stood before his hands—Gabriel having preceded them with the situation—he asked for the chest and informed them of what was in it. He commanded the earthworm, which took a hair and passed through the pearl, and he commanded a white worm, which took the thread and passed through the jasper. He called for water, and the girl would take water in her hand and place it in the other, then strike her face with it, while the boy, as he took it, struck his face with it. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verses 38–39:

﴿He said, "O chiefs, which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?"﴾ He intended by this to show her some of the marvels that Allah Most High had specially granted him, which indicate the greatness of His power and the truth of his claim to prophethood, and to test her intellect by presenting her throne in an unfamiliar form, so that he could see whether she would recognize it or deny it.

﴿before they come to me in submission﴾: for if she came as a Muslim, it would not be lawful to take her property except with her consent.

﴿A demon (ʿifrit) of the jinn said﴾: ʿifrit means a wicked, insolent rebel. ﴿of the jinn﴾ is an explanation of it, because a wicked, defiant man who subdues his peers is called ʿifrit. Its name was said to be Dhakwan or Sakhr. ﴿"I will bring it to you before you rise from your place"﴾: from your seat of judgment; he used to sit until midday. ﴿"And indeed I am strong for it, trustworthy"﴾: "for it" means for carrying it; "I will not diminish anything from it, nor alter it."

﴿Said he who had knowledge of the Scripture﴾: he was Asaf ibn Barkhiya, his vizier; or al-Khadir; or Jibril, peace be upon them both; or an angel whom God strengthened with it; or Sulayman, peace be upon him, himself. In that case the reference to him in this manner serves to indicate the nobility of knowledge and that this favour was by means of it. The address in ﴿I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you﴾ is to the ʿifrit (a powerful jinn), as if he (Sulayman) was slow to him, so he said this to him. Or he intended to show a miracle in its transfer: he challenged them first, then showed them that it was possible for him what was not possible for the ʿifrits of the jinn, let alone others. By "the Scripture" (al-Kitab) is meant the category of revealed books, or the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh). The word ﴿I bring﴾ in both places is suitable for both the verbal and the nominal sentence. "Al-tarf" is the moving of the eyelids for looking, so it is used in its place. Since the one who looks is described as sending out the glance, as in his saying:

*"And when you would send out your glance as a scout for your heart, one day the sights would wear you out."*

he is described as returning the glance, and the glance as returning. The meaning is that you send your glance toward something, and before you return it, I will have its throne brought before you. This is an extreme of speed and a figure of speech in it. ﴿Then when he saw it﴾, that is the throne, ﴿standing firm before him﴾, present in front of him.

﴿He said﴾, receiving the blessing with thanks, in the manner of the sincere servants of God the Exalted: ﴿This is of the bounty of my Lord﴾, which He bestowed upon me without any entitlement. The reference is to the ability to bring the throne within the time it takes the glance to return, from a distance of two months' journey, whether by himself or by another. The discussion of the possibility of its like has passed in the verse of "al-Isra". ﴿That He may test me: will I be thankful﴾, by recognising it as a favour from God the Exalted without any power or strength of my own, and fulfilling its right. ﴿Or will I be ungrateful﴾, by finding myself in the midst of it, or by falling short in performing its duties. Its position is accusative as a substitute for the "ya" (of the pronoun "to test me"). ﴿And whoever is thankful, he is thankful only for his own self﴾, because by it he draws to himself the lasting and increasing of the blessing, lightens from himself the burden of obligation, and protects it from the stain of ingratitude. ﴿And whoever is ungrateful﴾, then indeed my Lord is free of need of his thanks, ﴿Generous﴾ in bestowing upon him again.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verses 41–42:

﴿He said: "Disguise her throne for her"﴾ by changing its form and shape. ﴿"That we may see"﴾ is the response to the command (jawab al-amr). It is also read with the nominative (raf'), as a resumption (isti'naf, a new sentence).

﴿"Will she be guided, or will she be among those who are not guided?"﴾ That is, to knowledge of it, or to the right answer. It was also said that it means faith in Allah and His Messenger, when she saw her throne before her, although she had left it behind, its doors locked and guards assigned to it.

﴿So when she came, it was said: "Is your throne like this?"﴾ This was a comparison made to her, an added test of her intellect, since she had been described to him as having weak judgment.

﴿She said: "It is as if it were it"﴾. She did not say "It is it," because it might be something similar, and this is from the perfection of her intellect. ﴿"And we were given knowledge before her, and we were Muslims"﴾ is part of her speech. It is as if she thought that he intended by this to test her intellect and to display a miracle for her, so she said: "We were given knowledge of the perfection of Allah's power and of the truth of your prophethood before this situation," or the miracle is among the signs that had preceded. It was also said that it is part of the speech of Sulayman, peace be upon him, and his people, and that they joined it to her answer because it indicates her faith in Allah and His Messenger, since she allowed that it might be her throne, a strongly probable allowance. Its presence there is among the miracles which none can perform except Allah, Exalted is He, and which appear only at the hands of the prophets, peace be upon them. That is: "We were given knowledge of Allah, His power, and the truth of what He sent with him before her, and we were submitting to His judgment and had not ceased to follow His religion." Their purpose in this would be to speak of the blessing Allah had bestowed upon them through their precedence in this, as a thanks to Allah, Exalted is He.

Or, Allah barred her from worshipping it by granting her success in faith. ﴿إنَّها كانَتْ مِن قَوْمٍ كافِرِينَ﴾ "Indeed, she was from a disbelieving people." It is also read with a fatha (*bi-l-fath*) as a substitution (*al-ibdal*, substitution of one grammatical element for another) for the subject of *ṣaddahā* in the first reading. The meaning is: her upbringing among the disbelievers barred her, or the clause gives the reason for it.

﴿قِيلَ لَها ادْخُلِي الصَّرْحَ﴾ "It was said to her, 'Enter the palace.'" *Al-ṣarḥ* means the palace, and it is said to mean the courtyard of the house. ﴿فَلَمّا رَأتْهُ حَسِبَتْهُ لُجَّةً وكَشَفَتْ عَنْ ساقَيْها﴾ "So when she saw it, she thought it was a deep water, and she uncovered her shins." It is narrated that before her arrival he ordered the building of a palace whose courtyard was of white glass, made water flow beneath it, placed sea creatures in it, and set his throne in its middle, where he sat. When she saw it, she thought it was still water, so she uncovered her shins.

Ibn Kathir, according to the transmission of Qunbul, read *sa'aqayhā* with a hamza, analogizing it to its plural *suʼūq* and *aʼsuq* (shins, plural forms). ﴿قالَ إنَّهُ﴾ "He said, 'Indeed, it'" — that which you think is water. ﴿صَرْحٌ مُمَرَّدٌ﴾ "is a palace smoothed," meaning made smooth. ﴿مِن قَوارِيرَ﴾ "of glass," meaning of crystal glass.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 45–47:

﴿And We certainly sent to Thamud their brother Salih, [saying], "Worship Allah"﴾ — that is, "that worship Allah." It is also read with a damma on the nun, following the ba' (in the reading that is "ani-u'budu")...

﴿Then behold, they became two factions contending with one another.﴾ So they were suddenly struck by division and dispute: a group believed and a group disbelieved. The waw (in "fariqan") is for the whole of the two factions together.

﴿He said, "O my people, why do you seek to hasten the evil before the good?"﴾ — "the evil" meaning the punishment, so that you say, "Bring us what you threaten us with." — "before the good" meaning before repentance, so that you postpone it until the descent of the punishment; for they used to say, "If his threat is true, we will repent at that time." — ﴿Why do you not seek forgiveness of Allah﴾ before its descent.

﴿That perhaps you may receive mercy﴾ by accepting it, for it will not be accepted at that time.

﴿They said, "We consider you and those with you to be a bad omen."﴾ — we regard ourselves as ill-omened. — ﴿He said, "Your omen is with Allah"﴾ — that is, the cause of you, from which your evil came; — ﴿with Allah﴾ — that is, His decree, or your deeds recorded with Him. — ﴿Rather, you are a people being tested﴾ — tested by the alternation of ease and hardship. The shift from mentioning the source of their omen, which is the origin of what befalls them, to mentioning what it is that prompts it, is a change of subject (idrab).

﴿وَكانَ في المَدِينَةِ تِسْعَةُ رَهْطٍ﴾ "tis'atu anfusin" (nine persons). **Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verses 50–51:**

﴿And they schemed a scheme﴾ by this agreement. ﴿And We schemed a scheme﴾ by making it a means of their destruction. ﴿while they did not perceive﴾ it. It is related that Salih had a place of worship in al-Hijr, in a mountain pass, where he would pray. They said: "He claims that he will be finished with us within three [days], so let us finish with him and his family before the three [days]." So they went to the mountain pass to kill him, but a rock fell upon them in front of them and sealed the mouth of the pass over them, and they perished there, and the rest perished in their places by the Blast, as indicated by His saying:

﴿So see how was the end of their scheme: that We destroyed them and their people, all of them.﴾

As for ﴿كانَ﴾ (kana, "was"): if it is made defective (naqisa, incomplete), its predicate is ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ (kayfa, "how"), and ﴿أنّا دَمَّرْناهم﴾ (anna dammarnahum, "that We destroyed them") is either a new sentence (isti'naf) or the predicate of an omitted subject, not the predicate of ﴿كانَ﴾, because there is no returning pronoun (a'id). If you make it complete (tamma, complete), then ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ is a circumstantial (hal, state) accusative. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verses 54–55:

﴿And Lot⦆ — Mention Lot, or [it means] "And We sent Lot," indicating "And We had certainly sent upon him." ﴿When he said to his people⦆ is a *badal* (substitution, an apposition that restates the earlier term) according to the first reading, and a *zarf* (adverbial of time) according to the second. ﴿Do you indeed commit the abomination while you see?⦆ — you know its foulness through the sight of the heart, and committing ugly deeds while knowing their ugliness is worse. ﴿Do you indeed approach men with desire⦆ — this explains their committing the abomination. ﴿Say: "All praise is for Allah, and peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen."﴾ He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ), after relating to him the stories that demonstrate the perfection of His power and the greatness of His majesty, and the great signs with which He distinguished His messengers and the victory over their enemies, to praise Him and to send peace upon those of His servants whom He has chosen, in gratitude for what He has bestowed upon them. Or [He commanded him] to praise Him for teaching him what he did not know of their circumstances, and in recognition of their virtue, their right of precedence, and their striving in the religion. Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ya'qub read it with the letter ya (yushrikun, "they associate", in the third person).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 60:

﴿Amman﴾ (Is He Who), rather, "Amman" (is He Who) created the heavens and the earth, which are the origins of existing things and the sources of benefits. He [some reader] read "Amman" with the lightened pronunciation (al-takhfif), [treating it] as a substitute (badal) for "Allah." ﴿And sent down for you﴾, for your sake. ﴿from the sky water, and We caused to grow thereby gardens full of delight﴾. He shifted from the third person (al-ghaybah) to the first person (al-takallum) to emphasize that the act is exclusive to His Essence, and to draw attention to the fact that causing to grow such beautiful gardens, varied in kinds and distant in natures, from similar materials, is something no one other than Him is able to do, as He indicated by His saying: ﴿You could not have caused their trees to grow﴾. "Trees of the gardens" (shajar al-hada'iq) means the trees of orchards (al-basatin), from al-ihdaq, which is encompassing (al-ihatah). ﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾ Is there another who is associated with Him and made a partner to Him, when He alone is the One who creates and brings into being? It has been read as "a god" (ilahan), with a verb implied, such as "Do you call upon...?" or "Do you associate...?", and with a lengthened vowel placed between the two hamzas, and the second hamza pronounced as an intermediate sound (bayn bayn). ﴿Nay, but they are a people who swerve﴾ from the truth, which is monotheism (tawhid).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 61:

﴿Or who made the earth a place of settlement﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿or who created the heavens﴾, and [He] made it a place of settlement by bringing forth some of it from the water and leveling it, such that people and animals can settle upon it. ﴿And made within it rivers﴾, i.e. in its midst, flowing. ﴿And made for it firm mountains﴾, i.e. mountains in which minerals form and from whose lowlands springs gush forth. ﴿And made between the two seas﴾, i.e. the fresh and the salt, or the two gulfs of Persia and Rome, ﴿a barrier﴾, i.e. an isthmus (barzakh); its explanation has already passed in surah al-Furqan. ﴿Is there a god with Allah? Nay, most of them do not know﴾ the truth, so they associate partners with Him.

﴿Is He who answers the distressed one when he calls upon Him?﴾ The *mudtarr* (the distressed one) is the person whose extreme need compels him to seek refuge in God Most High from the state of *idtirar* (compulsion, dire need). The word is a *ifti'al* form derived from *darurah* (necessity). The *lam* in *al-mudtarr* is the *lam al-jins* (the lam of genus, indicating the category in general) and not the *lam al-istighraq* (the lam of totality, meaning all). Therefore it does not follow that every distressed person is answered. ﴿And removes the evil﴾, meaning He repels from the human being what harms him. ﴿And makes you successors (*khulafa'*) of the earth﴾, meaning successors upon it, in that He made you inherit its dwelling and its management from those who came before you. ﴿Is there a god with God?﴾, meaning the One who has bestowed upon you these general and particular blessings. ﴿Little is it that you remember﴾, meaning you remember His bounties, but only a little. *Ma* is *zā'idah* (superfluous, for emphasis), and by "littleness" is meant either non-existence or a degree of insignificance that negates the benefit. ﴿Or who guides you in the darknesses of the land and the sea?﴾, by the stars and the landmarks of the earth. ﴿Is He not (better) who originates creation and then repeats it?﴾ Although the disbelievers deny the repetition (of creation), they are refuted by the proofs that point to it. ﴿And who provides for you from the heaven and the earth?﴾ That is, by heavenly and earthly means. ﴿Is there a god along with God?﴾ Who does that? ﴿Say: Bring your proof﴾ that other than Him has power over any of that. ﴿If you are truthful﴾ in your associating (partners with Him), for perfect power is among the necessary attributes of divinity.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 65:

﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾. Because the exclusiveness of His, exalted is He, to complete and surpassing, all-encompassing power was mentioned, He followed it with what is almost a necessary consequence of it, namely His being alone in knowledge of the unseen. The exception (al-istithna', exception) is disjunctive (munqati', discontinuous), and the excepted noun is in the nominative according to the Tamimi dialect (al-lughah al-tamimiyyah, the dialect of the Banu Tamim), to indicate that, if He, exalted is He, is among those in the heavens and the earth, then among them are those who know the unseen, as an exaggeration in negating it from them. Or it is continuous (muttasil, connected), on the basis that what is meant by "those in the heavens and the earth" is by the connection of His knowledge to them and His being aware of them with the awareness of one present among them, so it includes Allah, exalted is He, and the people of knowledge among His creation; and it is either a relative (mawsul) or a descriptive (mawsuf) term. ﴿And they do not perceive when they will be resurrected﴾: when they will be raised. It is composed of "ayy" and "an" (ayyana, when), and it has been read with a kasra on the hamzah. The pronoun refers to "those" (man), and it has been said it refers to the disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 66:

﴿Rather, their knowledge has overtaken them concerning the Hereafter.﴾ When He negated from them knowledge of the unseen and reinforced this by negating their awareness of what would inevitably be their final state, He went to an extreme in this, turning away from that and explaining that what their means of knowledge, from proofs and signs, had reached and been perfected in is that the Resurrection is inevitably coming, though they do not know it as it should be known. ﴿Rather, they are in doubt about it﴾, like one who is bewildered in a matter and finds no evidence for it. ﴿Rather, they are blind to it﴾, not perceiving its proofs because their insight is defective. Although this is specific to the polytheists among those in the heavens (p-166) and the earth, it is attributed to all of them, just as the action of some is ascribed to all. The three transitions (idrabat) are a description of their states. It has been said that the first is a turning away from negating their awareness of the time of the Resurrection to describing them as having firmly established knowledge concerning the matter of the Hereafter, as a mockery of them. It has also been said that adraka here means "ended and vanished," from the saying "adraktu al-thamara" (I reached the fruit's ripeness), because that is its final point, at which it ceases to exist.

Nafi', Ibn Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read ﴿Rather, ittarak﴾ (بَلِ ادّارَكَ), meaning it followed in succession until it became firmly established, or it followed in succession until it ended, from "tadaraka Banu Fulan" (the sons of so-and-so followed one another) when they followed one another into destruction. Abu Bakr (in the transmission of 'Asim) reads "adraka" (أدْرَكَ). The original forms of both are tafa"ala and ifta"ala. It is also read "a-adraka" (أأدْرَكَ) and "am adraka" (أمْ أدْرَكَ) with two hamzas, "wa-'a-adraka" (وَءاأدْرَكَ) with an alif between them, "bal adraka" (بَلْ أدْرَكَ), "bal tadaraka" (بَلْ تَدارَكَ), "bala a-adraka" (بَلى أأدْرَكَ), and "am tadaraka" (أمْ تَدارَكَ). Whatever contains an explicit interrogative, or one implied from it, is a denial; whatever contains "bala" is an affirmation of their awareness and an explanation of it as perception, in mockery. What follows is a turning away from the explanation, emphasizing its negation and indicating that their awareness of it is that they are in doubt about it. ﴿Rather, they are blind to it﴾, or it is a rejection and denial of their awareness.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verses 67–68:

﴿And those who disbelieve say: "When we have become dust, and our fathers, shall we really be brought forth?"﴾ This is as an explanation of their bewilderment (ʿamah). The governing element (al-ʿamil) in "idhā" is what is indicated by ﴿shall we really be brought forth?﴾, and its meaning is "we will be brought forth," not "we are to be brought forth," because each of the interrogative hamzah, "inna" (indeed), and the lam (of emphasis) prevents it from governing what precedes it. The repetition of the hamzah is for emphasis in denial. By "bringing forth" (al-ikhraj) is meant bringing forth from the graves (al-ajdath), or from the state of annihilation to life. Nafiʿ read "idhā kunnā" with a single hamzah, pronounced with kasra, while Ibn ʿĀmir and al-Kisāʾi read "innanā la-mukhrajūna" with two nūns, as a declarative statement.

﴿Indeed, we and our fathers have been promised this before﴾, that is, before the promise of Muhammad (ﷺ). The placing of "hādhā" (this) before "naḥnu" (we) is because the intended subject of mention is the resurrection; where it is postponed, the intended subject is the one resurrected. ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾, which are like evening tales.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verses 69–70:

﴿Say: Travel through the earth and see how was the end of the criminals.﴾ This is a threat to them over their denial, and a warning that there will befall them the like of what befell those who denied before them. The expression "criminals" (al-mujrimin) is used for them so that it serves as a kindness (lutf) to the believers, deterring them from committing crimes.

﴿And do not grieve over them﴾ over their denial and their aversion. ﴿And do not be in distress﴾ in tightness of breast (haraj al-sadr). Ibn Kathir read it with a kasra on the dad (ḍīq), and both are two dialects (lughatan). It has also been read as ḍayyiq, meaning "a matter that is narrow" (amrun ḍayyiqun). ﴿on account of what they plot﴾ of their scheming, for indeed Allah will protect you from the people.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verses 71–72:

﴿They say, "When is this promise?"﴾ The promised punishment. ﴿If you are truthful.﴾

﴿Say: "Perhaps some of what you are hastening after has drawn close to you."﴾ It followed you and overtook you. The lam (*lām*) is extra, for emphasis, or the verb is understood to carry the meaning of a verb that takes the lam, like *dana* (drew near). It is also read with a fatḥa on the lam, which is a dialect (*lughah*) of the same word. ﴿Some of what you are hastening after.﴾ Its arrival, and it is the punishment of the day of Badr. *'Asā* (perhaps), *la'alla* (perhaps), and *sawfa* (surely) in the promises of kings are like certainty. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verses 73–75:

﴿And indeed, your Lord is full of bounty toward mankind﴾, by delaying their punishment for their sins. Al-fadl (bounty) and al-fadilah (bounty) mean al-afdal (favours), and its plural is fudul and fawadil. ﴿But most of them do not give thanks﴾, meaning they do not recognise the true value of the blessing in it, so they do not thank Him for it; rather, out of their ignorance, they hasten its occurrence.

﴿And indeed, your Lord knows what their breasts conceal﴾, meaning what they hide. It is also read with a fatha on the ta' (tukinnu), from kanantu, meaning I concealed. ﴿and what they reveal﴾, of your enmity, so that He will requite them for it.

﴿And there is not an unseen thing in the heaven and the earth﴾, hidden within them. These two (the heaven and the earth) are among the words that are predominantly used as adjectives, and the ta' in them (ghaibah and ghaibah) is for emphasis, as in al-rawiyah. Alternatively, they are nouns for that which is absent and concealed, like the ta' in 'afiyah and 'aqibah. ﴿except in a clear Book﴾, clear, or making clear what is in it to whoever looks into it. The intended meaning is the Preserved Tablet, or the Decree, by way of metaphor.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verses 76–78:

﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that about which they differ﴾ such as the (divine) likeness and transcendence (al-tashbih wa al-tanzih), the states of Paradise and Hell, and ʿUzayr and the Messiah.

﴿And indeed it is a guidance and a mercy for the believers﴾ for they are the ones who benefit from it.

﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them﴾ between the Children of Israel. ﴿by His judgment﴾ by what He judges, and it is the truth, by His wisdom; and what indicates this is that it was recited as "bi-hukmihi" (by His judgment). ﴿And He is the Mighty﴾ so His judgment is not reversed. ﴿the Knowing﴾ of the reality of what is being judged concerning it, and of its ruling.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 82:

﴿When the Word falls upon them﴾: that is, when the realization of its meaning draws near, namely what they were promised of resurrection and punishment. ﴿We shall bring forth for them a beast (dabbah) from the earth﴾: it is the Jassasah (the Beast of the Earth). It is narrated that its length is sixty cubits, that it has four legs, down and feathers, and two wings; no fleeing one escapes it, and no seeking one overtakes it. (p-168)

It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked where it would emerge from, and he said: "From the most sacred of the mosques in the sight of Allah, meaning the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram)."

﴿Speaks to them﴾: from speech (kalam). It has also been said it is from wounding (kalm), since it has been recited as "Takalmuhum."

It is narrated that it will emerge carrying the staff of Musa and the seal of Sulayman, peace be upon them both. It will strike with the staff on the face of the believer a white mark, so his face turns white, and with the seal on the nose of the disbeliever a black mark, so his face turns black.

﴿Because the people were not certain of Our signs﴾: of its emergence and all its conditions, for it is among the signs of Allah the Exalted. It has also been said the signs refer to the Qur'an. The Kufans recited "Anna al-nas" with a fatha. ﴿They were not certain﴾: they did not attain certainty. This is either a report of the meaning of its words, or a report of its speech regarding the saying of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, or the reason for its emergence, or its speaking with the preposition omitted.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verses 83–85:

﴿And on the Day We gather from every nation a company﴾ means the Day of Resurrection. ﴿of those who denied Our signs﴾ is an explanation of "company," meaning a company of deniers. The first ﴿min﴾ (from) is partitive (lil-tab'id), because "the nation of every prophet" and "the people of every generation" includes both those who affirmed and those who denied. ﴿Then they will be driven on﴾ means their first will be held back until their last, so that they catch up with one another. This is an expression for the great number of them and the vastness of their scattered ranks.

﴿Until, when they have come﴾ to the place of gathering. ﴿He will say, "Did you deny My signs while you did not encompass them in knowledge?"﴾ The waw is for the circumstantial clause (lil-hal), meaning: did you deny them hastily, without reflecting on them in a way that would give your knowledge comprehension of their reality and of whether they deserve affirmation or denial? Or it is for conjunction (lil-atf), meaning: you combined denying them with not applying your minds to verifying them. ﴿Or what was it that you were doing?﴾ That is, or what was it that you were doing after that? This is for rebuke, since they did nothing but deny out of ignorance, so they cannot say, "We did otherwise."

﴿And the word will fall upon them﴾ meaning the promised punishment will come upon them, which is their being thrown down into the Fire after that. ﴿Because of their wrongdoing﴾ meaning because of their wrongdoing, which is denying the signs of Allah. ﴿So they will not speak﴾ in excuse, being occupied with the punishment.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 86:

﴿Have they not seen﴾ so that monotheism (tawhid) might be established for them, and so that it would guide them to accept the possibility of the Resurrection (hashr) and the sending of the Messengers (ba'that al-rusul). This is because the alternation of light and darkness in a specific manner, which is not determined by its own essence, can only occur by the power of an Irresistible One (qahir). And whoever has power to replace darkness with light in one substance has power to replace death with life in the substances of bodies. And whoever made the day, so that they might see by it, a means among the means of their livelihood, [it follows that] He will surely not neglect that which is the basis of all their welfare in their livelihood and their return (ma'ad). ﴿That We made the night for them to rest in﴾ by sleep and repose. ﴿And the day to give sight﴾: its original form is "so that they might see in it," but this was intensified by making sight a state of the day's attributes with which it is inseparably associated. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾ because they indicate the three matters.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 87:**

﴿And [mention] the Day the Trumpet is blown﴾. [The word] *al-ṣūr* [is read as] *al-ṣuwar* (الصُّوَرِ), or *al-qarn* (the horn). It has been said that this is a metaphor for the resurrection of the dead through the rising of an army when a horn (*al-būq*) is sounded. ﴿So whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified﴾ from the terror, and it is expressed in the past tense to indicate the certainty of its occurrence. ﴿Except whom God wills﴾ from being terrified, by God making their hearts firm. It has been said they are Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil and Azra'il; it has been said they are the *hur* (companions of paradise), the guardians (*al-khazana*) and the bearers of the Throne; it has been said they are the martyrs; and it has been said they are Musa, peace be upon him, because he was struck unconscious once. Perhaps the intended meaning encompasses all of that.

﴿And all will come to Him﴾ present at the place of standing after the second blast, or submissively returning to His command. Hamza and Hafs read *atawhu* (أتَوْهُ) in the plural verb form, and it was also read *ataahu* (أتاهُ) in the singular, in agreement with the word *kull* (all). ﴿Humbled﴾ abased, and it was read *dakhirin* (دَخِرِينَ).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 88:

﴿And you see the mountains, you think them fixed,﴾ firm in their places. ﴿Yet they pass away as the clouds pass away﴾ in speed. This is because huge bodies, when they move in one uniform direction, hardly show their motion. ﴿The handiwork of Allah﴾ is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing itself, and it refers to the content of the preceding sentence, like His saying ﴿the promise of Allah﴾. ﴿Who perfected everything﴾ made its creation firm and arranged it as it should be. ﴿Indeed He is Aware of what you do﴾ knowing the outward and inward aspects of actions, and so He will requite you for them, as He said:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verses 89–90:

﴿Whoever brings a good deed, he will have better than it﴾ — because the noble (reward) is established for him in exchange for the base (deed), and the everlasting for the perishing, and seven hundredfold for one. It is also said: ﴿better than it﴾ means a good that comes to him from its direction, namely Paradise. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hisham read (khabeerun bima yaf'aluna, "He is Aware of what they do") with the ya' (third person), while the rest read it with the ta' (second person). ﴿And they, from the terror of that Day, will be safe﴾ — by this is meant the fear of the punishment of the Day of Resurrection. By the first (interpretation), what befalls a person of awe at what he sees of terrors and great matters is meant, and for this reason it encompasses both the disbeliever and the believer. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verses 91–92:

﴿Indeed, I have been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, who has made it sacred﴾. He commanded the Messenger ﷺ to say this to them after he had explained the origin and the return and described the conditions of the Resurrection, indicating that he had completed the call and it was complete, and that there remained for him only to occupy himself with its affair and to be absorbed in the worship of his Lord. Singling out Makkah with this attribution is an honouring of it and a magnification of its status. It has also been read as «allatī ḥarramahā» (the one which He made sacred).

﴿And to Him belongs everything﴾, in creation and dominion. ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾, those who submit, or those who remain steadfast upon the religion of Islam.

﴿And to recite the Qur'an﴾, and to be constant in its recitation, so that its truths may be revealed to me in its recitation little by little; or [it means] to follow it. It has also been read as «wa-ttlu ʿalayhim» (and recite to them) and «wa-an atlu» (and that I recite). ﴿Whoever is guided﴾ by following me in that, ﴿then he is guided only for himself﴾, for its benefits return to him.

﴿And whoever goes astray﴾ by opposing me. ﴿Say: I am only one of the warners﴾, so there is no burden upon me from the consequence of his straying, since the duty of the Messenger is only to convey, and I have conveyed.

"Say: All praise is due to Allah." Over the blessing of prophethood, or over what He taught me and enabled me to act upon. "He will show you His signs," the overpowering ones, "in this world, like the event of Badr and the emergence of the beast of the earth, or in the Hereafter. "So you will recognize them," that they are the signs of Allah, but when recognition will not benefit you. "And your Lord is not unaware of what you do." So do not suppose that the delay of your punishment is due to His being heedless of your deeds. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "ta'malūn" with the yā' (i.e., "ya'malūn").

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah Ta-Sin (Ta-Sin) will have ten good deeds recorded for him for each person who believed in Sulayman and denied him, and Hud, Salih, Ibrahim and Shu'ayb, and he will emerge from his grave calling out, 'There is no god but Allah.'"
